plate_findings.evidence: HE staining revealed tumefaction of the neural axon; giant axon labeled 'GA' with regenerating clusters (arrow)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Sural nerve biopsy from a patient with genetically confirmed giant axonal neuropathy; HE stain shows the hallmark giant axon (GA) with axonal tumefaction and regenerating clusters. B: Light-microscopy histology of the patient's sural nerve showing a giant axon (GA) alongside axonal atrophy and vascular wall thickening, consistent with giant axonal neuropathy. C: Immunohistochemical preparation of the patient's sural nerve corroborating the giant axon (GA) and showing mildly reduced myelinated fibers, as described in the in-text mentions. D: PAS-stained sural nerve section from the patient showing a giant axon (GA) with normal glycogen content, supporting the diagnosis of giant axonal neuropathy.
panels.attribution_text: Xu et al. Identification of Novel Compound Heterozygous Mutations in the GAN Gene of a Chinese Patient Diagnosed With Giant Axonal Neuropathy.. Frontiers in neuroscience 2020. doi:10.3389/fnins.2020.00085. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Microscopic examination of the patient’s sural nerve revealed a giant axon (GA). (A) HE staining revealed tumefaction of the neural axon and a few regenerating clusters (arrow). (B) Part of the axon atrophied mildly, and the vascular wall (arrow) was thickened and layered. (C) A myelinated nerve fiber (arrow) is slightly reduced. (D) No obvious increase in glycogen was observed.
in_text_mentions: On light microscopy, parts of the nerve fibers were observed to have tumid axis-cylinder spreads, in which the neurons were depleted of their myelin sheaths (Figure 2A). Medullated fibers were mildly reduced, and thin myelinated fibers were randomly spread (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemical staining corroborated the results (Figure 2C). Tissue cells, labeled by CD163, infiltrated the nerve fibers, while lymphocytes were not present, as shown by CD8 and CD20. The PAS staining showed normal glycogen content (Figure 2D). [raw subtype: classical GAN] E: Axial FLAIR MRI of Patient 5 at 14 years with classical GAN showing progression of bilateral cerebellar white matter hyperintensities. D–E Axial FLAIR images of Patient 5 at 9 (D) and 14 years old (E). At 9, only a mild hyperintense lesion was observed in the periaqueductal gray matter of the midbrain. By 14 years of age, hyperintense lesions had expanded to the bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. F Abdominal radiograph of Patient 5 at 9 years old revealing scoliosis and bowel gas accumulation.
